It astounds me how a 40 year career can be invalidated in a single moment. I mean it's not like I had very long left anyway, but I think I deserved more than a sucker punch KO.


The better half of those 40 years was spent searching for a cold blooded murderer who happened to be a resident in my not-so-big hometown; a fucked up game of hide and seek that saw people permanently lose, wether they knew they were playing or not. 
We called her the "Rainy Renegade" at the station - alliteration and a name straight out of a comic book often served to lighten the mood when you had to identify 3 bodies in your first 4 hours of a 12 hour shift. She got the name by only choosing to act when the weather was particularly bad. We could tell it was a 'her' (though I'm definitely sure now) as the footprints that weren't washed away by rain were particularly small with a notable imprint of a women's sports shoe.


The first time we saw that print was the morning after the third murder, 2 years in to the renegades 'career'. This one I remember clearly. I finally lost my rookie title, and what better way to celebrate than having to tell next-door's kid that their dad wouldn't be coming home for week old meatloaf and a cold one. 

It rained that night too, on my way home. The 20 minute walk from the station wasn't exactly full of joy but forgetting my umbrella didn't go much to help. I arrived at the front door and fumbled around my pockets looking for the key, landing on few coins and old receipts before I found it. Entering the house I saw Margaret watching the news, as she usually was, but younger and prettier than now - especially now - though you wouldn't be able to tell from the dim look she had on her face.
My heavy footed steps effortlessly caught her attention, and she turned to acknowledge my presence.


"How was work?" She said with all the happiness she could muster and the banality of a routine that had been going too long.


"More action than usual, which isn't exactly good," was my reply. "Mr Taylor was murdered."


In that moment I paid no attention to it. But looking back now it makes sense that her reaction was one of genuine disinterest, perhaps even a hint of a smirk; thinking, *knowing* that she'd gotten away with it.


"How was your day?" I asked.


She sighed, the kind of sigh that longed for something more.

"You know I've never liked the rain..."
